On the Reliability of Majority-Vote Pseudo-Labels in Test-Time Reinforcement Learning

Haoyu Wang    Ru Wang    Yuanyuan Wang    Jiaxian Guo    Mingming Gong
Abstract

Test-time reinforcement learning (TTRL) adapts pretrained language models to unlabeled target-domain data using self-generated pseudo-labels, whose reliability remains poorly understood. We analyze majority-vote supervision for TTRL with online Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) and decompose its error into population-majority bias and prompt-dependent finite-rollout variation. Because population-majority bias is generally unidentifiable without external supervision, we focus on mitigating the downstream effects of finite-rollout variation. We propose Prompt-Conditional Distributionally Robust DPO (PC-Dr.DPO), which conditions within-prompt robust reweighting on observed vote reliability to make updates from sampling-sensitive prompts more conservative. We further introduce a cache-based mechanism to reduce self-supervised forgetting during online adaptation. Across six mathematical and knowledge-intensive reasoning benchmarks and five model backbones, PC-Dr.DPO matches or outperforms the strongest TTRL baseline in 24 of 30 settings.

1 Introduction

Large language models (LLMs) have achieved strong performance across reasoning, planning, and knowledge-intensive tasks through large-scale pretraining and post-training alignment (OpenAI 2026; Google 2026; DeepSeek-AI 2026; Moonshot AI 2026; Qwen Team 2026). However, conventional post-training is predominantly offline: model parameters are fixed before deployment and cannot adapt to shifts in the test-time input distribution. This limitation is especially important in new or specialized domains, where labeled adaptation data and reliable external verifiers may be unavailable. It motivates test-time learning methods that adapt LLMs using unlabeled target-domain inputs and signals generated by the model itself.

Test-time reinforcement learning. Test-time reinforcement learning (TTRL) adapts a model on unlabeled target-domain prompts using self-generated rewards (Zuo et al. 2025). Existing approaches construct such rewards from either certainty-based signals, including prediction entropy and self-certainty (Prabhudesai et al. 2025; Zhao et al. 2025), or ensemble-based signals, including majority-vote consistency and agreement across alternative views of an input (Zuo et al. 2025; Zhang et al. 2025; Wang et al. 2025). Although these methods can improve reasoning without ground-truth labels, their success depends critically on the reliability of the resulting self-supervision.

Despite encouraging empirical results, this reliability remains incompletely understood. Prior work reports improvements even under imperfect or spurious rewards (Shao et al. 2025), whereas other studies highlight risks such as memorization and contamination (Wu et al. 2025b). Recent work further documents failure and collapse patterns in TTRL (He et al. 2026). Nevertheless, the lack of a formal framework characterizing when self-generated pseudo-labels are reliable limits the principled design of test-time adaptation algorithms.

In this work, we study majority-vote pseudo-labels for TTRL with online Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) (Rafailov et al. 2024; Pang et al. 2024; Ko et al. 2024). We identify two distinct sources of majority-vote error: (i) population-majority bias, which occurs when the behavior policy’s population-modal answer is incorrect, and (ii) finite-rollout variation, which occurs when the sampled majority differs from the population mode. The former cannot generally be identified or corrected without external supervision. The latter instead reflects sampling sensitivity and varies across prompts according to how decisively the behavior policy favors its modal answer over competing answers.

This prompt-level heterogeneity is important for preference construction. Figure 1 shows the distribution of the observed modal-answer fraction for Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B-Instruct on AMC. Although some prompts produce nearly unanimous rollout groups, others exhibit highly fragmented answer distributions. For the latter prompts, the selected pseudo-label is more sensitive to the particular rollout sample and may change under resampling.

Existing noise-robust preference optimization methods typically employ either a shared dataset-level noise model or a globally normalized robust objective over preference pairs (Mitchell 2023; Wu et al. 2025a). Consequently, they do not explicitly adapt the strength of robustness to the prompt-dependent reliability induced by finite-rollout sampling during test-time adaptation.

Our approach: PC-Dr.DPO. To address this mismatch, we propose Prompt-Conditional Distributionally Robust DPO (PC-Dr.DPO). PC-Dr.DPO performs robust reweighting separately within each prompt’s rollout group and adapts a prompt-specific robustness temperature using observed majority-vote reliability as a proxy for sampling sensitivity. For low-reliability prompts, the resulting reweighting emphasizes preference pairs already better satisfied by the current policy, yielding more conservative updates that mitigate the downstream optimization effects of finite-rollout errors. We further introduce a cache-based stabilization mechanism to reduce self-supervised forgetting during long-horizon online adaptation.

Our contributions are threefold:

  • •

    We develop a theoretical framework that separates population-majority bias from finite-rollout variation and characterizes how majority-vote errors propagate into the generalization risk of models trained on pseudo-preferences with a DPO-style objective.

  • •

    We propose PC-Dr.DPO, which uses prompt-level vote reliability to adapt within-prompt robust reweighting and reduce the influence of sampling-sensitive pseudo-labels. We further introduce a cache-based mechanism to mitigate self-supervised forgetting.

  • •

    We evaluate PC-Dr.DPO across six mathematical and knowledge-intensive reasoning benchmarks and five model backbones, matching or outperforming the strongest TTRL baseline in 24 of 30 settings.

2 Preliminaries

We briefly review the learning setting and the preference-optimization objectives that our analysis and method build upon. We keep the discussion minimal and focus on the notation used throughout the paper.

Problem Setup and RLVR Objective

Let πθ\pi_{\theta} denote a large language model parameterized by θ\theta, and let 𝒟\mathcal{D} be a dataset of question–answer pairs (x,a)(x,a). Given a prompt xx, the model generates a response trajectory y=(yt​1,…,yt​n)∼πθ(⋅∣x)y=(y_{t1},\ldots,y_{tn})\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x) autoregressively. We consider reasoning-style responses that contain intermediate steps (e.g., CoT (Wang et al. 2023)) and a final answer extracted by a deterministic function ans⁡(⋅)\mathrm{ans}(\cdot).

In the standard reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) setting (DeepSeek-AI 2025), we assume access to a verifier that compares the extracted answer with the ground-truth answer aa, yielding the binary reward r(x,y;a)=𝟏{ans(y)=a}r(x,y;a)=\mathbf{1}\{\mathrm{ans}(y)=a\}. Training with verifiable rewards is commonly formulated as KL-regularized policy optimization (Ouyang et al. 2022):

maxπθ𝔼x∼𝒟[𝔼y∼πθ(⋅∣x)[r(x,y)]−τDKL(πθ(⋅∣x)∥πref(⋅∣x))].\max_{\pi_{\theta}}\!\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}\!\Big[\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)}\big[r(x,y)\big]-\tau\,D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\big(\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\!\mid x)\,\|\,\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(\cdot\!\mid x)\big)\Big]. (1)

where πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} is a reference policy (typically an SFT model) and τ>0\tau>0 controls the strength of the KL regularization. In practice, several methods have been proposed to optimize (1), including PPO (Schulman et al. 2017), RLOO (Ahmadian et al. 2024), REMAX (Li et al. 2024), REINFORCE++ (Hu et al. 2025), and, most prominently, the GRPO family algorithms (Shao et al. 2024; Yu et al. 2025; Zheng et al. 2025).

Test-time self-reward via majority voting.

Unlike standard RLVR, the TTRL setting considered here assumes neither ground-truth answers nor an external verifier at adaptation time. Instead, the model constructs self-supervision from its own rollouts. For each prompt xx, the behavior policy samples mm independent responses {yi}i=1m\{y_{i}\}_{i=1}^{m} with yi∼πb(⋅∣x)y_{i}\sim\pi_{b}(\cdot\mid x) and forms the pseudo-label a^mv(x)=arg​maxa′∑i=1m𝟏{ans(yi)=a′}\widehat{a}_{\mathrm{mv}}(x)=\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{a^{\prime}}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\mathbf{1}\{\operatorname{ans}(y_{i})=a^{\prime}\} by majority voting over their extracted answers. This pseudo-label is used either to assign pseudo-rewards or to construct pseudo-preference pairs, treating matching rollouts as correct under the pseudo-label and the remaining rollouts as incorrect. Section 3 analyzes the reliability of this supervision under a DPO-style objective.

Direct Preference Optimization

Rather than performing explicit policy-gradient optimization, Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) (Rafailov et al. 2024) provides a supervised objective for optimizing the KL-regularized reward maximization problem using winner–loser preference pairs.

Let 𝒟pref\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{pref}} denote a dataset of preference tuples (x,yw,yl)(x,y_{w},y_{l}), where yw≻yly_{w}\succ y_{l} indicates that ywy_{w} is preferred to yly_{l} under prompt xx. DPO minimizes

ℒDPO​(θ)=−𝔼(x,yw,yl)∼𝒟pref​[hθ​(x,yw,yl)],\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DPO}}(\theta)=-\mathbb{E}_{(x,y_{w},y_{l})\sim\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{pref}}}\left[h_{\theta}(x,y_{w},y_{l})\right], (2)

where the per-pair log-preference score is

hθ​(x,yw,yl)=log⁡σ⁡(τ​gθ​(x,yw,yl)),h_{\theta}(x,y_{w},y_{l})=\log\sigma\!\left(\tau g_{\theta}(x,y_{w},y_{l})\right), (3)

and

gθ​(x,yw,yl)=log⁡πθ​(yw∣x)πref​(yw∣x)−log⁡πθ​(yl∣x)πref​(yl∣x).g_{\theta}(x,y_{w},y_{l})=\log\frac{\pi_{\theta}(y_{w}\mid x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y_{w}\mid x)}-\log\frac{\pi_{\theta}(y_{l}\mid x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y_{l}\mid x)}. (4)

Here, σ⁡(⋅)\sigma(\cdot) denotes the sigmoid function. We refer to gθg_{\theta} as the DPO margin and to hθh_{\theta} as the corresponding log-preference score.

Standard DPO operates on a fixed offline preference dataset. Online variants instead generate preference data iteratively from a behavior policy (Pang et al. 2024).

Distributionally Robust DPO

Dr.DPO (Wu et al. 2025a) applies KL-based distributionally robust reweighting to reduce the influence of pairs that are inconsistent with the current policy-relative preference ordering. Let s=(x,yw,yl)s=(x,y_{w},y_{l}) denote a preference sample and let pp be the empirical distribution over the preference dataset 𝒟pref\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{pref}}. Motivated by the dual form of a KL-constrained distributionally robust objective, Dr.DPO uses the fixed-temperature loss

ℒDrDPO​(θ)=−β​log⁡𝔼s∼p​[exp⁡(hθ​(s)β)],β>0,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DrDPO}}(\theta)=-\beta\log\mathbb{E}_{s\sim p}\left[\exp\!\left(\frac{h_{\theta}(s)}{\beta}\right)\right],\qquad\beta>0, (5)

where hθh_{\theta} is the DPO log-preference score defined in Equation (3).

Define the current pairwise preference probability as

νθ​(s):=σ⁡(τ​gθ​(s)),\nu_{\theta}(s):=\sigma\!\left(\tau g_{\theta}(s)\right),

so that hθ​(s)=log⁡νθ​(s)h_{\theta}(s)=\log\nu_{\theta}(s). The objective in Equation (5) induces the normalized exponential density ratio

wβ​(s)=exp⁡(hθ​(s)/β)𝔼s′∼p​[exp⁡(hθ​(s′)/β)],w_{\beta}(s)=\frac{\exp\!\left(h_{\theta}(s)/\beta\right)}{\mathbb{E}_{s^{\prime}\sim p}\left[\exp\!\left(h_{\theta}(s^{\prime})/\beta\right)\right]}, (6)

and hence

wβ​(s)∝νθ​(s)1/β.w_{\beta}(s)\propto\nu_{\theta}(s)^{1/\beta}.

The corresponding gradient is

∇θℒDrDPO​(θ)=−τ​𝔼s∼p​[wβ​(s)​(1−νθ​(s))​∇θgθ​(s)].\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DrDPO}}(\theta)=-\tau\,\mathbb{E}_{s\sim p}\left[w_{\beta}(s)\bigl(1-\nu_{\theta}(s)\bigr)\nabla_{\theta}g_{\theta}(s)\right]. (7)

Smaller values of β\beta produce a sharper exponential tilt toward pairs with larger current preference probabilities. The KL-DRO derivation and a detailed analysis of the effect of β\beta on the resulting gradient are provided in Appendix A.1.

3 Analysis of Majority-Vote Pseudo-Labels

We first analyze the reliability of majority-vote pseudo-labels in test-time reinforcement learning by separating two sources of error: population-majority bias, where the modal answer under the behavior policy is incorrect, and finite-rollout variation, where a sampled majority differs from that population mode.

Throughout this section, we condition on a fixed behavior policy πb\pi_{b} and adopt an i.i.d. preference-pair abstraction. Each sample s=(x,yw,yl)s=(x,y_{w},y_{l}) is independently constructed from mm rollouts for a sampled prompt using majority-vote preference labeling. The analysis applies separately to each online update, with πb\pi_{b} fixed to the rollout-generating policy at that update. Let 𝒫\mathcal{P} denote the resulting distribution over preference samples.

Generalization under Approximate Preference Labels

Let 𝒮\mathcal{S} be the preference-sample space and ℱ⊆{f:𝒮→ℝ}\mathcal{F}\subseteq\{f:\mathcal{S}\to\mathbb{R}\} a class of pairwise predictors. For s=(x,yw,yl)s=(x,y_{w},y_{l}), let z∈{0,1}z\in\{0,1\} denote the latent true preference label, with z=1z=1 corresponding to yw≻yly_{w}\succ y_{l}. Since the pair is ordered by the pseudo-labeling procedure, zz indicates whether the constructed ordering agrees with the true preference. We write p∗​(s):=(p∗​(z=1∣s),p∗​(z=0∣s))⊤∈Δ2p^{*}(s):=(p^{*}(z=1\mid s),p^{*}(z=0\mid s))^{\top}\in\Delta_{2}.

For DPO, the predictor is instantiated by the policy-relative margin

fθ​(s):=τ⁡[log⁡πθ​(yw∣x)πref​(yw∣x)−log⁡πθ​(yl∣x)πref​(yl∣x)],f_{\theta}(s):=\tau\!\left[\log\frac{\pi_{\theta}(y_{w}\mid x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y_{w}\mid x)}-\log\frac{\pi_{\theta}(y_{l}\mid x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y_{l}\mid x)}\right], (8)

where τ>0\tau>0 is the inverse-temperature parameter. The corresponding binary logistic loss is ℓDPO​(z,f)=−z​log⁡σ⁡(f)−(1−z)​log⁡σ⁡(−f)\ell_{\mathrm{DPO}}(z,f)=-z\log\sigma(f)-(1-z)\log\sigma(-f). Because the generalization result below requires a loss bounded in [0,1][0,1], we assume |f⁡(s)|≤M|f(s)|\leq M for every f∈ℱf\in\mathcal{F} and s∈𝒮s\in\mathcal{S}, and define ℓ⁡(z,f):=ℓDPO​(z,f)/log⁡(1+eM)∈[0,1]\ell(z,f):=\ell_{\mathrm{DPO}}(z,f)/\log(1+e^{M})\in[0,1]. This positive rescaling preserves empirical minimizers.

Let ℓ⁡(f⁡(s)):=(ℓ⁡(1,f⁡(s)),ℓ⁡(0,f⁡(s)))⊤\ell(f(s)):=(\ell(1,f(s)),\ell(0,f(s)))^{\top}. The true population risk is defined using p∗​(s)p^{*}(s). Since p∗​(s)p^{*}(s) is unavailable at test time, empirical optimization instead uses the pseudo-preference distribution p^​(s)∈Δ2\widehat{p}(s)\in\Delta_{2}:

R⁡(f)\displaystyle R(f) :=𝔼s∼𝒫​[p∗​(s)⊤​ℓ​(f⁡(s))],\displaystyle:=\mathbb{E}_{s\sim\mathcal{P}}\!\left[p^{*}(s)^{\top}\ell(f(s))\right], (9)
R~​(f,S)\displaystyle\widetilde{R}(f;S) :=1N​∑n=1Np^​(sn)⊤​ℓ​(f⁡(sn)),\displaystyle:=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\widehat{p}(s_{n})^{\top}\ell(f(s_{n})),

where S={sn}n=1N∼𝒫NS=\{s_{n}\}_{n=1}^{N}\sim\mathcal{P}^{N}.

Define the induced loss class and its covering complexity by

ℋ~\displaystyle\widetilde{\mathcal{H}} :={s↦p^​(s)⊤​ℓ​(f⁡(s)):f∈ℱ},\displaystyle:=\left\{s\mapsto\widehat{p}(s)^{\top}\ell(f(s)):\ f\in\mathcal{F}\right\}, (10)
ℳ~N\displaystyle\widetilde{\mathcal{M}}_{N} :=𝒩∞​(1N,ℋ~,2​N).\displaystyle:=\mathcal{N}_{\infty}\left(\tfrac{1}{N},\widetilde{\mathcal{H}},2N\right).

Following Menon et al. (2021), 𝒩∞​(ϵ,ℋ,n)\mathcal{N}_{\infty}(\epsilon,\mathcal{H},n) denotes the uniform ℓ∞\ell_{\infty} covering number of ℋ\mathcal{H} over samples of size nn. For brevity, define the sample-dependent generalization term

𝒢N​(f,δ,S):=O⁡(𝕍~N​(f,S)​log⁡(ℳ~N/δ)N+log⁡(ℳ~N/δ)N),\mathcal{G}_{N}(f,\delta;S):=O\!\left(\sqrt{\frac{\widetilde{\mathbb{V}}_{N}(f;S)\log(\widetilde{\mathcal{M}}_{N}/\delta)}{N}}+\frac{\log(\widetilde{\mathcal{M}}_{N}/\delta)}{N}\right), (11)

where 𝕍~N​(f,S)\widetilde{\mathbb{V}}_{N}(f;S) is the empirical variance of {p^​(sn)⊤​ℓ​(f⁡(sn))}n=1N\{\widehat{p}(s_{n})^{\top}\ell(f(s_{n}))\}_{n=1}^{N}.

Theorem 1 (Approximate preference distillation).

For any δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1), with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta over S∼𝒫NS\sim\mathcal{P}^{N}, every f∈ℱf\in\mathcal{F} satisfies

R⁡(f)≤R~​(f,S)+12​𝔼s∼𝒫​[‖p^​(s)−p∗​(s)‖1]+𝒢N​(f,δ,S).R(f)\leq\widetilde{R}(f;S)+\frac{1}{2}\,\mathbb{E}_{s\sim\mathcal{P}}\!\left[\left\|\widehat{p}(s)-p^{*}(s)\right\|_{1}\right]+\mathcal{G}_{N}(f,\delta;S). (12)

The second term in Equation (12) is the expected total-variation distance between the pseudo-preference and true conditional preference distributions. Unlike 𝒢N​(f,δ,S)\mathcal{G}_{N}(f,\delta;S), this mismatch need not vanish as NN increases and therefore contributes persistently to the bound when pseudo-label error is systematic. The complete proof is given in Appendix A.2.

Majority-Vote Error Decomposition

To expose the central mechanism, we consider a binary answer space and assume deterministic ground-truth preferences. For any pair with distinct final answers, the true preference distribution p∗​(s)p^{*}(s) assigns probability one to the response whose extracted answer equals the ground-truth answer a⋆​(x)a^{\star}(x). Define the per-rollout correctness probability and the population-majority answer under the behavior policy πb\pi_{b} by

ρb​(x)\displaystyle\rho_{b}(x) :=Prπb⁡(ans⁡(y)=a⋆​(x)∣x),\displaystyle:=\Pr_{\pi_{b}}\!\left(\operatorname{ans}(y)=a^{\star}(x)\mid x\right), (13)
ab∞​(x)\displaystyle a_{b}^{\infty}(x) :=arg⁡maxa​Prπb​(ans⁡(y)=a∣x).\displaystyle:=\arg\max_{a}\Pr_{\pi_{b}}\!\left(\operatorname{ans}(y)=a\mid x\right).

In the binary setting, ab∞​(x)=a⋆​(x)a_{b}^{\infty}(x)=a^{\star}(x) when ρb​(x)>1/2\rho_{b}(x)>1/2, whereas the population majority is incorrect when ρb​(x)<1/2\rho_{b}(x)<1/2. We assume that the rollout count mm is odd, so the sampled majority is unique, and adopt a fixed tie-breaking rule for the population boundary case ρb​(x)=1/2\rho_{b}(x)=1/2.

Given rollouts y1,…,ym∼i.i.d.πb(⋅∣x)y_{1},\ldots,y_{m}\overset{\mathrm{i.i.d.}}{\sim}\pi_{b}(\cdot\mid x), define the sampled-majority answer by

a^m,b(x):=argmaxa∑i=1m{ans(yi)=a}.\widehat{a}_{m,b}(x):=\arg\max_{a}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\mathbf{1}\!\left\{\operatorname{ans}(y_{i})=a\right\}. (14)

A response agreeing with a^m,b​(x)\widehat{a}_{m,b}(x) is treated as the winner, whereas a response containing the alternative answer is treated as the loser. Thus, the pseudo-preference distribution assigns probability one to the constructed ordering, so p^​(s)=(1,0)⊤\widehat{p}(s)=(1,0)^{\top}.

Define the conditional majority-vote error probability by

Um,b​(x):=Pr⁡(a^m,b​(x)≠a⋆​(x)∣x),U_{m,b}(x):=\Pr\!\left(\widehat{a}_{m,b}(x)\neq a^{\star}(x)\mid x\right), (15)

Under the binary deterministic-preference abstraction, the expected total-variation term in Theorem 1 equals 𝔼x​[Um,b​(x)]\mathbb{E}_{x}[U_{m,b}(x)], as shown in Appendix A.3. Consequently, with the same probability 1−δ1-\delta, every f∈ℱf\in\mathcal{F} satisfies

R⁡(f)≤R~​(f,S)+𝔼x​[Um,b​(x)]+𝒢N​(f,δ,S),R(f)\leq\widetilde{R}(f;S)+\mathbb{E}_{x}\!\left[U_{m,b}(x)\right]+\mathcal{G}_{N}(f,\delta;S), (16)

where the expectation is taken with respect to the prompt marginal induced by 𝒫\mathcal{P}.

Population Bias and Finite-Rollout Variation

We now decompose the majority-vote error into population-majority bias and finite-rollout variation:

Bb​(x)\displaystyle B_{b}(x) :=𝟏{ab∞(x)≠a⋆(x)},\displaystyle:=\mathbf{1}\left\{a_{b}^{\infty}(x)\neq a^{\star}(x)\right\}, (17)
Vm,b​(x)\displaystyle V_{m,b}(x) :=Pr⁡(a^m,b​(x)≠ab∞​(x)∣x).\displaystyle:=\Pr\!\left(\widehat{a}_{m,b}(x)\neq a_{b}^{\infty}(x)\mid x\right).
Proposition 1 (Exact majority-error decomposition).

Under the binary-answer abstraction, for every prompt xx,

Um,b​(x)\displaystyle U_{m,b}(x) =(1−Bb​(x))​Vm,b​(x)+Bb​(x)​(1−Vm,b​(x))\displaystyle=\bigl(1-B_{b}(x)\bigr)V_{m,b}(x)+B_{b}(x)\bigl(1-V_{m,b}(x)\bigr)
=Bb​(x)+(1−2​Bb​(x))​Vm,b​(x).\displaystyle=B_{b}(x)+\bigl(1-2B_{b}(x)\bigr)V_{m,b}(x). (18)
Lemma 1 (Majority-vote concentration).

For every prompt xx with ρb​(x)≠1/2\rho_{b}(x)\neq 1/2,

Vm,b​(x)≤exp⁡(−2​m​|ρb​(x)−12|2).V_{m,b}(x)\leq\exp\!\left(-2m\left|\rho_{b}(x)-\tfrac{1}{2}\right|^{2}\right). (19)

Combining Proposition 1 and Lemma 1, for any γ>0\gamma>0,

ρb​(x)≥12+γ\displaystyle\rho_{b}(x)\geq\tfrac{1}{2}+\gamma ⟹Um,b​(x)≤e−2​m​γ2,\displaystyle\Longrightarrow U_{m,b}(x)\leq e^{-2m\gamma^{2}}, (20)
ρb​(x)≤12−γ\displaystyle\rho_{b}(x)\leq\tfrac{1}{2}-\gamma ⟹Um,b​(x)≥1−e−2​m​γ2.\displaystyle\Longrightarrow U_{m,b}(x)\geq 1-e^{-2m\gamma^{2}}.
Corollary 1 (Generalization under majority-vote supervision).

Suppose that |ρb​(x)−1/2|≥γ>0\left|\rho_{b}(x)-1/2\right|\geq\gamma>0 almost surely, and let

αb:=Prx⁡(ρb​(x)<12)=𝔼x​[Bb​(x)].\alpha_{b}:=\Pr_{x}\!\left(\rho_{b}(x)<\tfrac{1}{2}\right)=\mathbb{E}_{x}[B_{b}(x)].

Then

|𝔼x​[Um,b​(x)]−αb|≤e−2​m​γ2.\left|\mathbb{E}_{x}[U_{m,b}(x)]-\alpha_{b}\right|\leq e^{-2m\gamma^{2}}. (21)

Consequently, with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta over S∼𝒫NS\sim\mathcal{P}^{N}, every f∈ℱf\in\mathcal{F} satisfies

R⁡(f)≤R~​(f,S)+αb+e−2​m​γ2+𝒢N​(f,δ,S).R(f)\leq\widetilde{R}(f;S)+\alpha_{b}+e^{-2m\gamma^{2}}+\mathcal{G}_{N}(f,\delta;S). (22)

Proofs are provided in Appendix A.4–A.5.

Interpretation.

For a fixed behavior policy, αb\alpha_{b} captures population-majority bias and does not decrease with the rollout count mm. By contrast, finite-rollout variation decays exponentially in mm. Increasing mm can therefore stabilize the sampled majority but cannot correct an incorrect population majority. Appendix C.1 empirically illustrates this distinction using Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B-Instruct on AMC with m∈{16,32,64}m\in\{16,32,64\}.

4 Our Method: Prompt-Conditional Dr.DPO

The preceding analysis separates majority-vote error into population-majority bias and finite-rollout variation under a simplified binary-answer abstraction. Without external supervision, the former is generally unidentifiable: an incorrect but decisive population majority may still appear highly reliable. We therefore focus on mitigating the downstream optimization effects of finite-rollout variation. Our method uses observed vote concentration as a proxy for sampling sensitivity and adjusts the strength of robust reweighting separately for each prompt.

Prompt-Conditional Robust Objective

Let pp denote the empirical distribution over preference samples s=(x,yw,yl)s=(x,y_{w},y_{l}). Standard Dr.DPO applies a globally normalized exponential tilt with a shared temperature across all preference pairs. To account for prompt-dependent reliability, we instead consider the conditional uncertainty set

𝒰={q:q(x)=p(x),KL(q(⋅∣x)∥p(⋅∣x))≤ηx,∀x}.\mathcal{U}=\left\{q:q(x)=p(x),\ \mathrm{KL}\!\left(q(\cdot\mid x)\,\|\,p(\cdot\mid x)\right)\leq\eta_{x},\ \forall x\right\}.

This set keeps the prompt marginal fixed while permitting prompt-specific reweighting of the conditional pair distribution. Given the DPO score hθh_{\theta} defined in Equation (3), the corresponding robust score is

supq∈𝒰𝔼s∼q​[hθ​(s)].\sup_{q\in\mathcal{U}}\mathbb{E}_{s\sim q}\left[h_{\theta}(s)\right]. (23)

Because q⁡(x)=p⁡(x)q(x)=p(x), the inner optimization decomposes across prompts:

𝔼x∼p⁡(x)[supqx:KL(qx∥p(⋅∣x))≤ηx𝔼s∼qx[hθ(s)]].\mathbb{E}_{x\sim p(x)}\left[\sup_{\begin{subarray}{c}q_{x}:\,\mathrm{KL}(q_{x}\|p(\cdot\mid x))\leq\eta_{x}\end{subarray}}\mathbb{E}_{s\sim q_{x}}\left[h_{\theta}(s)\right]\right]. (24)

Applying KL-ball duality to each conditional problem gives

𝔼x∼p⁡(x)[infβx>0{βxηx+βxlog𝔼s∼p(⋅∣x)[exp(hθ​(s)βx)]}].\mathbb{E}_{x\sim p(x)}\left[\inf_{\beta_{x}>0}\left\{\beta_{x}\eta_{x}+\beta_{x}\log\mathbb{E}_{s\sim p(\cdot\mid x)}\left[\exp\!\left(\frac{h_{\theta}(s)}{\beta_{x}}\right)\right]\right\}\right]. (25)

Let βx=βx⋆​(ηx)\beta_{x}=\beta_{x}^{\star}(\eta_{x}) denote the prompt-specific dual temperature associated with the prescribed radius ηx\eta_{x}. Following the fixed-temperature formulation of Dr.DPO, we hold βx\beta_{x} fixed during the policy update and omit the additive term βx​ηx\beta_{x}\eta_{x}, which is independent of θ\theta. This yields the prompt-conditional score

𝔼x∼p⁡(x)[βxlog𝔼s∼p(⋅∣x)[exp(hθ​(s)βx)]].\mathbb{E}_{x\sim p(x)}\left[\beta_{x}\log\mathbb{E}_{s\sim p(\cdot\mid x)}\left[\exp\!\left(\frac{h_{\theta}(s)}{\beta_{x}}\right)\right]\right]. (26)

The temperature βx\beta_{x} controls the sharpness of the conditional exponential tilt. Smaller values concentrate weight on pairs with larger current DPO scores, whereas larger values produce weights closer to uniform within the prompt group.

Finite-sample objective.

At adaptation step tt, rollouts are sampled from πt−1\pi_{t-1}, which also serves as the reference policy: πref=πt−1\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}=\pi_{t-1}. For each prompt xx, let

Pt​(x)={sx​i}i=1Nx,sx​i=(x,yw,i,yl,i),P_{t}(x)=\{s_{xi}\}_{i=1}^{N_{x}},\qquad s_{xi}=(x,y_{w,i},y_{l,i}),

denote the resulting preference pairs. The prompt-conditional objective is

ℒPC​-​DrDPO​(θ,x)=−βx​log⁡[1Nx​∑i=1Nxexp⁡(hθ​(sx​i)βx)].\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{PC\text{-}DrDPO}}(\theta;x)=-\beta_{x}\log\left[\frac{1}{N_{x}}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{x}}\exp\!\left(\frac{h_{\theta}(s_{xi})}{\beta_{x}}\right)\right]. (27)

Unlike standard Dr.DPO, which normalizes globally over preference pairs, Equation (27) normalizes within each prompt group. Let

νx​i:=σ⁡(τ​gθ​(sx​i)),hθ​(sx​i)=log⁡νx​i.\nu_{xi}:=\sigma\!\left(\tau g_{\theta}(s_{xi})\right),\qquad h_{\theta}(s_{xi})=\log\nu_{xi}.

The induced weights and gradient are

w¯x​i​(βx)\displaystyle\overline{w}_{xi}(\beta_{x}) =νx​i1/βx∑k=1Nxνx​k1/βx,\displaystyle=\frac{\nu_{xi}^{1/\beta_{x}}}{\sum_{k=1}^{N_{x}}\nu_{xk}^{1/\beta_{x}}}, (28)
∇θℒPC​-​DrDPO​(θ,x)\displaystyle\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{PC\text{-}DrDPO}}(\theta;x) =−τ∑i=1Nxw¯x​i(βx)(1−νx​i)∇θgθ(sx​i).\displaystyle=-\tau\sum_{i=1}^{N_{x}}\overline{w}_{xi}(\beta_{x})(1-\nu_{xi})\nabla_{\theta}g_{\theta}(s_{xi}). (29)

As βx→0+\beta_{x}\to 0^{+}, the objective approaches −maxi⁡hθ​(sx​i)-\max_{i}h_{\theta}(s_{xi}) and the weights concentrate on the highest-scoring pairs; as βx→∞\beta_{x}\to\infty, the weights become uniform over Pt​(x)P_{t}(x).

Reliability-Conditioned Temperature

For each prompt xx, let {yi}i=1m∼i.i.d.πt−1(⋅∣x)\{y_{i}\}_{i=1}^{m}\overset{\mathrm{i.i.d.}}{\sim}\pi_{t-1}(\cdot\mid x), and let a^m,t−1​(x)\widehat{a}_{m,t-1}(x) denote the sampled modal-answer. We define

κ(x):=1m∑i=1m𝟏{ans(yi)=a^m,t−1(x)}.\kappa(x):=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\mathbf{1}\left\{\operatorname{ans}(y_{i})=\widehat{a}_{m,t-1}(x)\right\}. (30)

The modal-answer fraction κ⁡(x)\kappa(x) does not determine whether the resulting pseudo-label is correct. Instead, it serves as an observable proxy for finite-rollout stability.

We set

βx=βbase​κ​(x),βbase>0.\beta_{x}=\beta_{\mathrm{base}}\kappa(x),\qquad\beta_{\mathrm{base}}>0. (31)

Thus, weaker observed majorities receive smaller temperatures and sharper within-prompt reweighting, whereas stronger majorities receive smoother weights closer to uniform averaging. The temperature is computed from the rollout group and held fixed during policy differentiation.

Proposition 2 (Effect of prompt-conditional temperature).

Fix θ\theta and a prompt group Pt​(x)={sx​i}i=1NxP_{t}(x)=\{s_{xi}\}_{i=1}^{N_{x}}. Let νx​i:=νθ​(sx​i)\nu_{xi}:=\nu_{\theta}(s_{xi}) and define

Ax​(β):=∑i=1Nxw¯x​i​(β)​(1−νx​i).A_{x}(\beta):=\sum_{i=1}^{N_{x}}\overline{w}_{xi}(\beta)(1-\nu_{xi}). (32)

Then Ax​(β)A_{x}(\beta) is nondecreasing in β\beta. Moreover, if ‖∇θgθ​(sx​i)‖≤G\|\nabla_{\theta}g_{\theta}(s_{xi})\|\leq G for all ii, then

‖∇θℒPC​-​DrDPO​(θ,x)‖≤τ​G​Ax​(βx).\left\|\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{PC\text{-}DrDPO}}(\theta;x)\right\|\leq\tau GA_{x}(\beta_{x}). (33)

Consequently, with the current pairwise scores held fixed, decreasing βx\beta_{x} decreases this upper bound on the prompt-level update magnitude.

The proof is provided in Appendix A.1. Intuitively, a smaller temperature places greater weight on pairs with larger νx​i\nu_{xi}, for which the residual factors 1−νx​i1-\nu_{xi} are smaller. This moderates the gradient-norm upper bound for prompts whose sampled majorities appear less stable.

Cache-Based Stabilization Against Self-Forgetting

Some prompts become degenerate during online adaptation: all sampled rollouts produce the same final answer, so no valid winner–loser pair can be constructed and Pt​(x)=∅P_{t}(x)=\emptyset. We exclude such prompts from the preference update.

When a prompt first becomes degenerate, we cache its rollout completions, denoted by 𝒞⁡(x)\mathcal{C}(x). Because all cached completions share the same final answer, we denote this answer by a𝒞​(x)a_{\mathcal{C}}(x). If the prompt is encountered again and its new sampled-majority answer disagrees with a𝒞​(x)a_{\mathcal{C}}(x), we discard the newly generated pseudo-preference pairs and instead apply the cache loss

ℒcache(θ;x)=−1|𝒞⁡(x)|∑y∈𝒞⁡(x)logπθ(y∣x).\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{cache}}(\theta;x)=-\frac{1}{|\mathcal{C}(x)|}\sum_{y\in\mathcal{C}(x)}\log\pi_{\theta}(y\mid x). (34)

This replay-style safeguard discourages a later conflicting pseudo-label from overwriting previously stable self-supervision.

Overall Objective and Update Rule

For a mini-batch of prompts ℬt\mathcal{B}_{t}, let ℬcache\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{cache}} denote the prompts that trigger the cache rule, and define

ℬnorm:={x∈ℬt∖ℬcache:Pt​(x)≠∅}.\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{norm}}:=\left\{x\in\mathcal{B}_{t}\setminus\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{cache}}:P_{t}(x)\neq\emptyset\right\}.

The complete update objective is

ℒt​(θ)=\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{t}(\theta)= 1|ℬnorm|​∑x∈ℬnormℒPC​-​DrDPO​(θ,x)\displaystyle\frac{1}{|\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{norm}}|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{norm}}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{PC\text{-}DrDPO}}(\theta;x) (35)
+μ⋅1|ℬcache|∑x∈ℬcacheℒcache(θ;x),\displaystyle+\mu\cdot\frac{1}{|\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{cache}}|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{cache}}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{cache}}(\theta;x),

where μ≥0\mu\geq 0 controls the relative weight of the cache loss. (When ℬcache=∅\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{cache}}=\emptyset, the second term is omitted.)

At each adaptation step, we perform one or more gradient updates on Equation (35) and set the resulting policy as πt\pi_{t}. Using πref=πt−1\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}=\pi_{t-1} keeps each DPO update local to the behavior policy that generated the corresponding rollout data.

Trajectory-score-based answer selection.

Majority voting over discrete answers ignores within-answer heterogeneity. To incorporate the model’s internal preference signal, we compute an implicit DPO score for each rollout using successive-policy likelihood ratios. At update step t≥2t\geq 2, we treat πt−2\pi_{t-2} as a lagged reference and define

rt​(y∣x):=log⁡πt−1​(y∣x)πt−2​(y∣x).r_{t}(y\mid x):=\log\frac{\pi_{t-1}(y\mid x)}{\pi_{t-2}(y\mid x)}. (36)

We aggregate these scores by extracted final answer and select a^m,t−1score(x)=arg​maxa∑i:ans⁡(yi)=art(yi∣x)\widehat{a}^{\,\mathrm{score}}_{m,t-1}(x)=\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{a}\sum_{i:\operatorname{ans}(y_{i})=a}r_{t}(y_{i}\mid x), with ties resolved by a fixed rule. Rollouts producing the selected answer are treated as winners, whereas those producing other answers are treated as losers when constructing Pt​(x)P_{t}(x). Frequency-based majority voting is recovered by assigning every trajectory unit score. At the first adaptation step, when πt−2\pi_{t-2} is unavailable, we use frequency-based selection. This rule affects only preference construction and leaves Equation (35) unchanged.

5 Experimental Setup

Models.

We evaluate PC-Dr.DPO across multiple architectures and model scales, including Qwen2.5-1.5B/3B/7B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B-Instruct (Qwen Team 2025). We also evaluate Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct (Meta AI 2024) to assess whether the method generalizes across model families. We use instruction-tuned variants throughout to avoid chat-template mismatches under distribution shift, ensuring that performance differences primarily reflect test-time adaptation rather than formatting artifacts.

Benchmarks.

We compare PC-Dr.DPO with three TTRL baselines: the certainty-based method RENT (Prabhudesai et al. 2025) and the ensemble-based methods TTRL and Co-Reward (Zuo et al. 2025; Zhang et al. 2025). Evaluation covers four mathematical-reasoning benchmarks—AIME24, AIME25, AMC23, and MATH500 (Hendrycks et al. 2021)—and two knowledge-intensive reasoning benchmarks, GPQA-Diamond (Rein et al. 2023) and MMLU-Pro (Wang et al. 2024). Due to computational constraints, we evaluate MMLU-Pro on its mathematics subset, which contains 1,351 examples.

Test-time adaptation is performed on the full evaluation set, or on the official test split when available. All methods use the same fixed adaptation budget for each benchmark, and we report accuracy at the final checkpoint rather than selecting the best intermediate checkpoint. This protocol avoids favoring methods that improve early but subsequently collapse, reflecting the practical setting in which the onset of degradation is not known in advance.

Implementation details.

We implement PC-Dr.DPO in the veRL framework (Sheng et al. 2025) and run all experiments on a single node with eight NVIDIA H100 GPUs. We use Adam with a constant learning rate of 5×10−75\times 10^{-7}. For PC-Dr.DPO, we sample m=32m=32 rollouts per prompt and construct eight preference pairs for each policy update. For TTRL and Co-Reward, we likewise sample 32 rollouts per prompt and downsample them to eight training examples. For RENT, we directly sample eight rollouts per prompt. This keeps the number of examples entering each policy update consistent across methods. Rollouts are generated with temperature T=0.8T=0.8 and nucleus-sampling parameter p=0.9p=0.9. Additional hyperparameter settings are provided in Appendix B.1.

Main Results

Table 1 reports test-time adaptation accuracy under Avg@32 evaluation. Avg@32 denotes the mean correctness over 32 sampled rollouts generated with temperature T=0.8T=0.8 and top-p=0.9p=0.9. Results marked with ∗\ast indicate adaptation runs that collapsed before the final checkpoint; representative failure cases are provided in Appendix C.2.

Across 24 of the 30 model–benchmark combinations, PC-Dr.DPO matches or outperforms the strongest TTRL baseline. These results demonstrate the benefit of prompt-conditional reweighting for reducing the optimization effects of finite-rollout variation during test-time adaptation.

Ablation Studies

We conduct two ablation studies. First, we evaluate the contributions of the reliability-conditioned temperature and score-based majority selection using Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct on AMC and MATH500. Second, we study the effect of the rollout-caching mechanism using Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct on MATH500.

Temperature and majority selection.

Table 2 isolates the two principal design choices in PC-Dr.DPO. The constant-temperature variant replaces the reliability-conditioned schedule in Equation (31) with βx=βbase\beta_{x}=\beta_{\mathrm{base}}. The frequency-based variant replaces score-based majority selection with standard answer-frequency voting while retaining the adaptive temperature.

We further ablate the cache-replay mechanism using Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct on MATH500. During adaptation, replaying previously cached preference groups periodically anchors the policy to earlier self-consistent solutions and mitigates self-supervised forgetting. Removing this mechanism reduces Avg@32 accuracy from 58.4%58.4\% to 56.3%56.3\%. Additional analysis is provided in Appendix C.3.

Qualitative Analysis

We analyze Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B-Instruct on AMC to better understand the dynamics of test-time adaptation under majority-vote supervision. Both TTRL and PC-Dr.DPO derive reinforcement signals from majority-voted responses among the model’s own rollouts. The set of problems solved by the initial rollout majority therefore provides a useful reference for measuring how effectively adaptation converts self-consistent solutions into improved policy performance.

Empirically, we observe two distinct behaviors. For some problems, adaptation successfully recovers solutions contained in the initial majority-vote-solvable set and may additionally solve previously unsolved problems, potentially through transfer of shared reasoning structure across related prompts. For others, adaptation fails to recover the initially available solutions and may even degrade performance. We attribute this failure mode to the repeated reinforcement of incorrect population-majority pseudo-labels, which can introduce systematic bias into the adapted policy. Additional trajectories and representative examples on MATH500 across multiple model backbones are provided in Appendix C.4.

6 Conclusion

We analyzed majority-vote supervision in online-DPO TTRL, separating population-majority bias from prompt-dependent finite-rollout variation. To mitigate the latter, we introduced PC-Dr.DPO with reliability-conditioned within-prompt reweighting and cache replay. Across six benchmarks and five backbones, PC-Dr.DPO matches or exceeds the strongest TTRL baseline in 24 of 30 settings.

Appendix A Detailed Proofs

KL-DRO Derivation and Gradient Behavior

Let s=(x,yw,yl)s=(x,y_{w},y_{l}) denote a preference sample and recall

gθ​(s)\displaystyle g_{\theta}(s) =log⁡πθ​(yw∣x)πref​(yw∣x)−log⁡πθ​(yl∣x)πref​(yl∣x),\displaystyle=\log\frac{\pi_{\theta}(y_{w}\mid x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y_{w}\mid x)}-\log\frac{\pi_{\theta}(y_{l}\mid x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y_{l}\mid x)}, (37)
νθ​(s)\displaystyle\nu_{\theta}(s) =σ(τgθ(s)),hθ(s)=logνθ(s).\displaystyle=\sigma\!\left(\tau g_{\theta}(s)\right),\qquad h_{\theta}(s)=\log\nu_{\theta}(s).

Let pp denote the empirical distribution over the preference pairs.

Consider the distributionally robust score

supq:KL(q∥p)≤η𝔼s∼q[hθ(s)],\sup_{q:\,\mathrm{KL}(q\|p)\leq\eta}\mathbb{E}_{s\sim q}\left[h_{\theta}(s)\right], (38)

where η≥0\eta\geq 0 controls the allowable deviation from pp. Assume q≪pq\ll p and let r=d​q/d​pr=dq/dp be the corresponding density ratio. Then r≥0r\geq 0, 𝔼p​[r]=1\mathbb{E}_{p}[r]=1, and

KL(q∥p)=𝔼p[rlogr]=𝔼p[ϕ(r)],ϕ(r):=rlogr−r+1.\mathrm{KL}(q\|p)=\mathbb{E}_{p}[r\log r]=\mathbb{E}_{p}[\phi(r)],\qquad\phi(r):=r\log r-r+1.

Hence, Equation (38) is equivalent to

supr≥0𝔼p​[r​hθ]s.t.𝔼p​[ϕ⁡(r)]≤η,𝔼p​[r]=1.\sup_{r\geq 0}\mathbb{E}_{p}[rh_{\theta}]\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\mathbb{E}_{p}[\phi(r)]\leq\eta,\qquad\mathbb{E}_{p}[r]=1. (39)

=β​η−α+β​𝔼p​[r​hθ+αβ−ϕ⁡(r)].\displaystyle=\beta\eta-\alpha+\beta\,\mathbb{E}_{p}\left[r\frac{h_{\theta}+\alpha}{\beta}-\phi(r)\right]. (40)

For β>0\beta>0, the convex conjugate of ϕ⁡(r)=r​log⁡r−r+1\phi(r)=r\log r-r+1 is

ϕ∗​(u)=supr≥0{r​u−ϕ⁡(r)}=eu−1,\phi^{*}(u)=\sup_{r\geq 0}\{ru-\phi(r)\}=e^{u}-1,

with maximizer r∗​(u)=eur^{*}(u)=e^{u}. Maximizing Equation (40) over rr therefore gives

g⁡(α,β)=β​η−α+β​𝔼p​[e(hθ+α)/β−1].g(\alpha,\beta)=\beta\eta-\alpha+\beta\,\mathbb{E}_{p}\left[e^{(h_{\theta}+\alpha)/\beta}-1\right]. (41)

Differentiating with respect to α\alpha yields

and thus

α∗=−β​log⁡𝔼p​[ehθ/β].\alpha^{*}=-\beta\log\mathbb{E}_{p}\left[e^{h_{\theta}/\beta}\right]. (42)

Substituting Equation (42) into Equation (41) gives

supq:KL(q∥p)≤η𝔼q[hθ]=infβ>0{βη+βlog𝔼p[ehθ/β]}.\sup_{q:\,\mathrm{KL}(q\|p)\leq\eta}\mathbb{E}_{q}[h_{\theta}]=\inf_{\beta>0}\left\{\beta\eta+\beta\log\mathbb{E}_{p}\left[e^{h_{\theta}/\beta}\right]\right\}. (43)

For any β>0\beta>0, the associated exponentially tilted distribution is

qθ,β​(s)=p⁡(s)​exp⁡(hθ​(s)/β)𝔼s′∼p​[exp⁡(hθ​(s′)/β)].q_{\theta,\beta}(s)=p(s)\frac{\exp\!\left(h_{\theta}(s)/\beta\right)}{\mathbb{E}_{s^{\prime}\sim p}\left[\exp\!\left(h_{\theta}(s^{\prime})/\beta\right)\right]}. (44)

Under the fixed-temperature approximation, we associate each prescribed robustness radius η\eta with a temperature β⋆​(η)\beta^{\star}(\eta), which is treated as independent of θ\theta and held fixed during the policy update.

Fixed-temperature objective.

Assume that β⋆​(η)\beta^{\star}(\eta) minimizes the dual objective in Equation (43) under this fixed-temperature parameterization. Then

ℒDrDPO​(θ)=−β​log⁡𝔼s∼p​[exp⁡(hθ​(s)β)].\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DrDPO}}(\theta)=-\beta\log\mathbb{E}_{s\sim p}\left[\exp\!\left(\frac{h_{\theta}(s)}{\beta}\right)\right]. (46)

wβ​(s):=exp⁡(hθ​(s)/β)𝔼s′∼p​[exp⁡(hθ​(s′)/β)].w_{\beta}(s):=\frac{\exp\!\left(h_{\theta}(s)/\beta\right)}{\mathbb{E}_{s^{\prime}\sim p}\left[\exp\!\left(h_{\theta}(s^{\prime})/\beta\right)\right]}. (47)

Consider a finite collection of preference pairs 𝒮={si}i=1N\mathcal{S}=\{s_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N} and let

dd​t​∑i=1Nw¯i​(t)​νi=Covw¯​(t)⁡(νi,log⁡νi)≥0,\frac{d}{dt}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\overline{w}_{i}(t)\nu_{i}=\operatorname{Cov}_{\overline{w}(t)}\left(\nu_{i},\log\nu_{i}\right)\geq 0, (53)

Total-Variation Identity for Deterministic Binary Preferences

Lemma (Total-variation identity for deterministic binary preferences).

Assume both the true and pseudo-preference distributions are deterministic. Then

12‖p^(s)−p∗(s)‖1=𝟏{a^m,b(x)≠a⋆(x)}.\frac{1}{2}\left\|\hat{p}(s)-p^{*}(s)\right\|_{1}=\mathbf{1}\left\{\widehat{a}_{m,b}(x)\neq a^{\star}(x)\right\}. (65)

Consequently,

12​𝔼s∼𝒫​[‖p^​(s)−p∗​(s)‖1]=𝔼x​[Um,b​(x)].\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}_{s\sim\mathcal{P}}\left[\left\|\hat{p}(s)-p^{*}(s)\right\|_{1}\right]=\mathbb{E}_{x}\left[U_{m,b}(x)\right]. (66)
Proof.

Let z∗​(s)∈{0,1}z^{*}(s)\in\{0,1\} denote the true preference label and let z^​(s)∈{0,1}\widehat{z}(s)\in\{0,1\} denote the pseudo-preference label induced by the sampled-majority answer. Under the deterministic binary construction,

p∗​(s)=ez∗​(s),p^​(s)=ez^​(s),p^{*}(s)=e_{z^{*}(s)},\qquad\hat{p}(s)=e_{\widehat{z}(s)},

where e0=(1,0)⊤e_{0}=(1,0)^{\top} and e1=(0,1)⊤e_{1}=(0,1)^{\top}. Hence,

12​‖p^​(s)−p∗​(s)‖1\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\left\|\hat{p}(s)-p^{*}(s)\right\|_{1} =12​‖ez^​(s)−ez∗​(s)‖1\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\left\|e_{\widehat{z}(s)}-e_{z^{*}(s)}\right\|_{1}
=𝟏{z^(s)≠z∗(s)}\displaystyle=\mathbf{1}\left\{\widehat{z}(s)\neq z^{*}(s)\right\}
=𝟏{a^m,b(x)≠a⋆(x)}.\displaystyle=\mathbf{1}\left\{\widehat{a}_{m,b}(x)\neq a^{\star}(x)\right\}. (67)

Taking expectations and applying the law of total expectation gives

12​𝔼s∼𝒫​[‖p^​(s)−p∗​(s)‖1]\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}_{s\sim\mathcal{P}}\left[\left\|\hat{p}(s)-p^{*}(s)\right\|_{1}\right] =𝔼x​[Pr⁡(a^m,b​(x)≠a⋆​(x)∣x)]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{x}\left[\Pr\!\left(\widehat{a}_{m,b}(x)\neq a^{\star}(x)\mid x\right)\right]
=𝔼x​[Um,b​(x)].\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{x}\left[U_{m,b}(x)\right]. (68)

Proof of Majority-Vote Concentration

Proof.

Fix a prompt xx and let

Zi:=𝟏{ans(yi)=a⋆(x)},yi∼i.i.d.πb(⋅∣x),Z_{i}:=\mathbf{1}\left\{\operatorname{ans}(y_{i})=a^{\star}(x)\right\},\qquad y_{i}\overset{\mathrm{i.i.d.}}{\sim}\pi_{b}(\cdot\mid x),

for i=1,…,mi=1,\ldots,m. Conditional on xx, the variables Z1,…,ZmZ_{1},\ldots,Z_{m} are i.i.d. Bernoulli random variables satisfying

𝔼⁡[Zi∣x]=ρb​(x).\mathbb{E}[Z_{i}\mid x]=\rho_{b}(x).

Define their empirical mean by

Z¯m:=1m​∑i=1mZi.\overline{Z}_{m}:=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m}Z_{i}.

Under the binary-answer abstraction, if ρb​(x)>1/2\rho_{b}(x)>1/2, then the population-majority answer is a⋆​(x)a^{\star}(x). Therefore, disagreement between the sampled and population majorities implies Z¯m≤1/2\overline{Z}_{m}\leq 1/2. Hence, Hoeffding’s inequality gives

Vm,b​(x)\displaystyle V_{m,b}(x) ≤Pr⁡(Z¯m≤12∣x)\displaystyle\leq\Pr\!\left(\overline{Z}_{m}\leq\frac{1}{2}\mid x\right)
=Pr⁡(Z¯m−ρb​(x)≤−(ρb​(x)−12)|x)\displaystyle=\Pr\!\left(\overline{Z}_{m}-\rho_{b}(x)\leq-\left(\rho_{b}(x)-\frac{1}{2}\right)\middle|x\right)
≤exp⁡(−2​m​(ρb​(x)−12)2).\displaystyle\leq\exp\!\left(-2m\left(\rho_{b}(x)-\frac{1}{2}\right)^{2}\right). (69)

If instead ρb​(x)<1/2\rho_{b}(x)<1/2, then the population-majority answer is incorrect. Disagreement with that population majority implies Z¯m≥1/2\overline{Z}_{m}\geq 1/2, and Hoeffding’s inequality yields

Vm,b​(x)\displaystyle V_{m,b}(x) ≤Pr⁡(Z¯m≥12∣x)\displaystyle\leq\Pr\!\left(\overline{Z}_{m}\geq\frac{1}{2}\mid x\right)
=Pr⁡(Z¯m−ρb​(x)≥12−ρb​(x)|x)\displaystyle=\Pr\!\left(\overline{Z}_{m}-\rho_{b}(x)\geq\frac{1}{2}-\rho_{b}(x)\middle|x\right)
≤exp⁡(−2​m​(12−ρb​(x))2).\displaystyle\leq\exp\!\left(-2m\left(\frac{1}{2}-\rho_{b}(x)\right)^{2}\right). (70)

For even mm, these inclusions remain valid under any deterministic tie-breaking rule. Combining the two cases gives

Vm,b​(x)≤exp⁡(−2​m​|ρb​(x)−12|2).V_{m,b}(x)\leq\exp\!\left(-2m\left|\rho_{b}(x)-\frac{1}{2}\right|^{2}\right).

For completeness, under the binary abstraction,

Um,b​(x)=Bb​(x)+(1−2​Bb​(x))​Vm,b​(x).U_{m,b}(x)=B_{b}(x)+\bigl(1-2B_{b}(x)\bigr)V_{m,b}(x).

Thus, when ρb​(x)≥1/2+γ\rho_{b}(x)\geq 1/2+\gamma, we have Bb​(x)=0B_{b}(x)=0 and

Um,b​(x)=Vm,b​(x)≤e−2​m​γ2.U_{m,b}(x)=V_{m,b}(x)\leq e^{-2m\gamma^{2}}.

When ρb​(x)≤1/2−γ\rho_{b}(x)\leq 1/2-\gamma, we have Bb​(x)=1B_{b}(x)=1 and

Um,b​(x)=1−Vm,b​(x)≥1−e−2​m​γ2.U_{m,b}(x)=1-V_{m,b}(x)\geq 1-e^{-2m\gamma^{2}}.

Under the binary-answer abstraction, the exact majority-error decomposition gives

Um,b​(x)−Bb​(x)=(1−2​Bb​(x))​Vm,b​(x),U_{m,b}(x)-B_{b}(x)=\bigl(1-2B_{b}(x)\bigr)V_{m,b}(x), (71)

αb:=𝔼x​[Bb​(x)]=Prx⁡(ρb​(x)<12).\alpha_{b}:=\mathbb{E}_{x}[B_{b}(x)]=\Pr_{x}\!\left(\rho_{b}(x)<\frac{1}{2}\right).

Vm,b​(x)≤e−2​m​γ2almost surely.V_{m,b}(x)\leq e^{-2m\gamma^{2}}\qquad\text{almost surely}.

Hence,

|𝔼x​[Um,b​(x)]−αb|\displaystyle\left|\mathbb{E}_{x}[U_{m,b}(x)]-\alpha_{b}\right| =|𝔼x​[Um,b​(x)−Bb​(x)]|\displaystyle=\left|\mathbb{E}_{x}\left[U_{m,b}(x)-B_{b}(x)\right]\right|
≤𝔼x​[|Um,b​(x)−Bb​(x)|]\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{E}_{x}\left[\left|U_{m,b}(x)-B_{b}(x)\right|\right]
=𝔼x​[Vm,b​(x)]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{x}[V_{m,b}(x)]
≤e−2​m​γ2.\displaystyle\leq e^{-2m\gamma^{2}}. (73)

In particular,

𝔼x​[Um,b​(x)]≤αb+e−2​m​γ2.\mathbb{E}_{x}[U_{m,b}(x)]\leq\alpha_{b}+e^{-2m\gamma^{2}}. (74)

The majority-vote generalization bound gives, with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta over S∼𝒫NS\sim\mathcal{P}^{N}, simultaneously for every f∈ℱf\in\mathcal{F},

R⁡(f)≤R~​(f,S)+𝔼x​[Um,b​(x)]+𝒢N​(f,δ,S).R(f)\leq\widetilde{R}(f;S)+\mathbb{E}_{x}[U_{m,b}(x)]+\mathcal{G}_{N}(f,\delta;S).

Substituting Equation (74) yields

R⁡(f)≤R~​(f,S)+αb+e−2​m​γ2+𝒢N​(f,δ,S),R(f)\leq\widetilde{R}(f;S)+\alpha_{b}+e^{-2m\gamma^{2}}+\mathcal{G}_{N}(f,\delta;S),

which proves the result. ∎

Appendix B Implementation Details

Hyperparameters

For PC-Dr.DPO, ppo_micro_batch_size is set equal to the number of preference pairs constructed per prompt, ensuring that each prompt group remains intact during within-prompt robust reweighting.

Appendix C More Results

Effect of the Rollout Count

Figure 3 compares rollout counts m∈{16,32,64}m\in\{16,32,64\} for Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B-Instruct on AMC. Larger rollout counts reduce variation in the sampled pseudo-labels and yield more stable validation trajectories. This observation is consistent with our analysis: increasing mm suppresses finite-rollout variation.

Self-Reinforcing Collapse under Incorrect Population Majorities

Figure 4 shows the adaptation dynamics of Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct on AIME25. The sampled pseudo-label accuracy remains close to zero, indicating that most prompt-level supervision signals are incorrect. Nevertheless, the modal-answer fraction increases throughout training and eventually approaches one. The policy therefore becomes more internally consistent without becoming more correct. Repeated optimization against these increasingly decisive but incorrect pseudo-labels reinforces population-majority bias, while validation Avg@32 accuracy ultimately collapses to zero.

Analysis of Cache Replay

Figure 5 examines the cache-replay mechanism using Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct on MATH500. During adaptation, the cache accumulates preference groups associated with previously mastered prompts and periodically replays them in subsequent updates. As shown in Figure 5(a), replay events revisit a subset of these earlier solutions throughout training.

Figures 5(b)–(c) compare adaptation with and without cache replay. Without replay, pseudo-label accuracy gradually decreases and validation performance exhibits larger regressions. Replaying cached preference groups anchors the policy to earlier self-consistent solutions, improving the retention of previously acquired behavior and raising final Avg@32 accuracy from 56.3%56.3\% to 58.4%58.4\%. These results support the use of cache replay as a mechanism for mitigating self-supervised forgetting during online adaptation.

Additional Adaptation Dynamics on MATH500

Figure 6 presents additional adaptation trajectories on MATH500 for Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B-Instruct. For each run, the problems solved by the initial rollout majority define a fixed reference set. The left panels report the fraction of this set recovered by the current policy, the middle panels show the difference between the current number of solved problems and the initial majority-vote reference, and the right panels decompose the currently solved problems into recovered and newly discovered solutions.

Across both backbones, adaptation progressively recovers most solutions available in the initial reference set. Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct recovers approximately 90%90\% of the initially solvable problems, whereas Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B-Instruct approaches nearly complete recovery. Both models also solve some problems outside the initial reference set, showing that the initial majority-vote-solvable set is not a strict performance upper bound. Nevertheless, incomplete recovery remains, indicating that some initially available solutions are lost during adaptation. These trajectories illustrate the competing effects of solution recovery, cross-prompt transfer, and degradation induced by systematic pseudo-label errors, which can steer policy updates away from previously available solutions.
